title: Running Containers
summary: Start containers with docker run, publish ports, override defaults, then list, inspect, exec into, stop and remove them.

blocks.text: `docker run` (alias of `docker container run`) creates a new container from an image and starts it, pulling the image first if it isn't present. Usage: `docker run [OPTIONS] IMAGE [COMMAND] [ARG...]`.

rows: Run in the background and print the container ID
Give the container a name; otherwise the daemon picks a random one such as vibrant_cannon
Keep STDIN open / allocate a pseudo-TTY; `-it` gives an interactive shell
Remove the container (and its anonymous volumes) when it exits

blocks.text:
docker run --name <name> -d <image>
docker stop <name>
docker rm <name>
docker run -it <image>            # interactive session

items: A detached container exits when its root process exits. Don't run something like `service nginx start` as the command: it returns at once, so the container stops.
A stopped container keeps its filesystem by default. `docker start` restarts it with its earlier changes intact; `docker ps -a` lists stopped containers too.
Combining `--restart` with `--rm` is an error.

blocks.text: Containers are isolated, so you can't reach their apps directly. Publishing a port at container creation sets up a forwarding rule from a host port to a container port with `-p` (`--publish`).

docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx             # HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT
docker run -d -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 nginx   # HOST_IP:HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT
docker run -p 80 nginx                     # host port picked by Docker (ephemeral)
docker run -P nginx                        # publish every EXPOSEd port

items: The `EXPOSE` instruction in an image only documents a port; exposed ports aren't published unless you ask.
`-P` (`--publish-all`) maps all exposed ports to ephemeral host ports, handy for avoiding port conflicts in dev and test.
With an ephemeral port, `docker ps` shows the chosen mapping in the PORTS column, for example `0.0.0.0:54772->80/tcp`.

blocks.text: Without a host IP, a published port listens on all interfaces (`0.0.0.0` / `::`), so anything reaching the machine can connect. Prefix `127.0.0.1:` to keep it local, especially for databases.
A container runs the program its image is configured with, but `docker run` flags let you change ports, environment, resources and the command itself.

docker run -d -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret -p 5433:5432 postgres   # 2nd instance on another host port
docker run --env-file .env postgres env                             # many variables from a file
docker run -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret --memory="512m" --cpus="0.5" postgres
docker run -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret postgres docker-entrypoint.sh -h localhost -p 5432

items: `-e foo=bar` sets one variable; `--env-file` avoids a long list of `-e` flags.
Containers have no resource limits by default. `--memory` caps memory and `--cpus` sets a CPU quota (0.5 = half a core). `docker stats` shows live usage.
Anything after the image name replaces the image's default command.

blocks.text: Running two copies of the same database? Keep the container port and change only the host port: `-p 5432:5432` for one, `-p 5433:5432` for the other.
`docker ps` is an alias of `docker container ls` (also `docker container list` and `docker container ps`). By default it shows only running containers.

rows: Show writable-layer size and virtual size

blocks.text: Valid `status` values: created, restarting, running, removing, paused, exited, dead.
`docker logs <container>` fetches the logs that exist when you run it. Add flags to stream or trim them.

docker logs -f <container>           # keep streaming STDOUT and STDERR
docker logs -n <lines> <container>   # --tail; default is all
docker logs -t <container>           # add timestamps
docker logs --since 42m <container>  # relative or absolute time
`docker exec` runs a **new** command inside a running container, in its default working directory.

docker exec -it <container> sh                    # interactive shell
docker exec -d <container> touch /tmp/execWorks   # in the background
docker exec -e VAR_A=1 <container> env            # extra env for this process only
docker exec -it -w /root <container> pwd          # other working dir
docker exec -it <container> sh -c "echo a && echo b"

items: The command must be an executable. A quoted chain like `"echo a && echo b"` fails; wrap it in `sh -c`.
It only runs while the container's PID 1 is running, and isn't rerun if the container restarts.
Exec into a paused container fails until you unpause it.
`docker stop <container>` sends the main process **SIGTERM**, then **SIGKILL** after a grace period.
Change the first signal with the `STOPSIGNAL` Dockerfile instruction, `--stop-signal` on `docker run`, or `-s` on `docker stop`.
`-t, --timeout` sets the wait in seconds; `-1` waits forever. The daemon default is **10 seconds** on Linux and 30 on Windows.
Without `--network`, a container joins the built-in **default bridge** network. It can reach outside services through masquerading.
On the default bridge, containers reach each other by IP only, **not by name**.
On a **user-defined** network, containers reach each other by IP or by container name, using Docker's embedded DNS server at `127.0.0.11`.
On a bridge network, every container port is reachable from the host and from containers on the same network. Use `-p` to reach it from outside the host or from other bridge networks.
A container's hostname defaults to its ID; override it with `--hostname`.

blocks.text:
docker network create -d bridge my-net
docker run --network=my-net -it busybox

rows: No network isolation from the Docker host
Fully isolated from host and other containers
External VLANs / appear as devices on the host's network

flashcards.front: What does docker run do if the image isn't available locally?
flashcards.back: It pulls the image, then creates and starts the container.
Publishes every port the image EXPOSEs to an ephemeral host port.

flashcards.front: How do you load many environment variables at once?
Flags that limit a container's memory and CPU?

How do you follow a container's logs live?
How do you open an interactive shell in a running container?
Which signals does docker stop send, and what is the default timeout on Linux?
flashcards.back: SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after the grace period. Default 10 seconds on Linux.

flashcards.front: Can containers on the default bridge network resolve each other by name?
flashcards.back: No, only by IP. User-defined networks give name resolution.

questions.stem: You want host port 8080 to forward to port 80 inside an nginx container. Which command is correct?

options.explanation: The format is HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT.
This maps host port 80 to container port 8080: the reverse.
-P publishes all exposed ports to ephemeral host ports; it takes no port mapping.
--expose exposes a container port without publishing it to the host.

questions.stem: A database container was started with -p 5432:5432. Why is that a concern on a shared network?

options.text: Without a host IP the port is published on all interfaces, so any traffic reaching the machine can connect
options.explanation: Use 127.0.0.1:5432:5432 to keep it local.

options.text: The port is only reachable from other containers
options.explanation: Published ports are reachable from outside the host.

options.text: Docker picks a random host port instead of 5432
options.explanation: Docker picks a port only when HOST_PORT is omitted.

options.text: Publishing disables the container's network isolation entirely
options.explanation: It sets up a forwarding rule for that port; isolation otherwise stays in place.

questions.stem: Ports declared with EXPOSE in an image are published to the host automatically.

options.explanation: Exposed ports aren't published by default.
You must use -p, or -P to publish all exposed ports.

questions.stem: You need a second Postgres container next to one already using host port 5432. What is the simplest fix?

options.explanation: Change the host port and keep the container port 5432.
The host port 5432 still conflicts, and Postgres listens on 5432 in the container.
--cpus limits CPU; it doesn't change ports.

options.text: Stop the first container; Docker allows only one container per image
options.explanation: You can run many containers from one image.

questions.stem: Which docker run flags set environment variables in the container? Select 2.

options.explanation: -e foo=bar sets foo inside the container.
Loads variables from a file such as .env.
Sets a memory limit.
Attaches the container to a network.

questions.stem: docker run -d -p 80:80 my_image service nginx start starts nginx, but the container stops at once. Why?

options.text: The root process (service nginx start) returns, and a detached container exits when its root process exits
options.explanation: Run nginx in the foreground instead, e.g. nginx -g 'daemon off;'.
-d runs the container in the background; it keeps running while the root process runs.
Publishing is unrelated to the container exiting.

options.text: The restart policy defaults to always
options.explanation: The default policy is no.

questions.stem: Which restart policy keeps a container down after a daemon restart if you stopped it manually?

options.explanation: Like always, but a stopped container isn't restarted even when the daemon restarts.
A manually stopped container comes back when the daemon restarts.
Restarts only on a non-zero exit code; that's not the rule this question asks about.
Never restarts automatically, even after a crash.

questions.stem: By default, a container's filesystem persists after the container exits, and docker start brings it back with its changes intact.

options.explanation: Unless you used --rm, the container and its filesystem stay until removed.
Only --rm removes the container automatically on exit.

questions.stem: You need the IDs of all exited containers to pass to docker rm. Which command prints them?

options.explanation: -q prints only IDs and the filter selects exited containers.
-s shows sizes, and without -a or a filter only running containers are listed.
-l shows only the latest created container.
Shows full output but still only running containers.

questions.stem: docker exec -it web "echo a && echo b" fails. What works?

options.text: docker exec -it web sh -c "echo a && echo b"
options.explanation: The command must be an executable; a shell runs the chained string.

options.text: docker exec -d web "echo a && echo b"
options.explanation: Running in the background doesn't fix a quoted chained command.

options.text: docker logs web "echo a && echo b"
options.explanation: docker logs fetches output; it doesn't run commands.

options.text: docker exec -w / web "echo a && echo b"
options.explanation: -w changes the working directory only.

questions.stem: Which statements about docker exec are true? Select 2.

options.text: It runs only while the container's primary process (PID 1) is running
options.explanation: Stated on the exec reference.

options.text: Variables set with -e apply only to the exec'd process
options.explanation: Other processes in the container don't see them.

options.text: The command reruns automatically if the container restarts
options.explanation: It isn't restarted when the container restarts.

options.text: It works on a paused container
options.explanation: It fails with an error until you unpause the container.

questions.stem: docker stop app takes about 10 seconds and the process is then killed. What is happening?

options.text: The process ignored SIGTERM, so Docker sent SIGKILL after the default 10-second timeout
options.explanation: Linux containers default to 10 seconds; adjust with -t.

options.text: docker stop always sends SIGKILL first
options.explanation: SIGTERM (or the configured stop signal) is sent first.

options.text: The image's restart policy is delaying the stop
options.explanation: Restart policies decide restarts after exit, not stop timing.

options.text: The daemon's default timeout is 30 seconds on Linux
options.explanation: 30 seconds is the Windows default; Linux is 10.

questions.stem: Container api must reach container db by name. What is needed?

options.text: Attach both to the same user-defined network
options.explanation: User-defined networks resolve container names via the embedded DNS server.

options.text: Leave both on the default bridge network
options.explanation: The default bridge allows IP-only communication.
none isolates the container completely.
Publishing exposes a port outside the host; it doesn't give name resolution.

questions.stem: A container started without --network joins the default bridge network.

options.explanation: The default bridge is the built-in network used when --network is omitted.
It joins the default bridge.

questions.stem: Which network driver removes network isolation between a container and the Docker host?

options.explanation: The host driver shares the host's network.
none fully isolates the container.
overlay connects multiple Docker daemons.
macvlan makes containers appear as devices on the host's network.
